title: Explaining Complexity Out Loud in an Interview
oneLiner: A seven-step template for stating time and space and the reason for each, with weak and strong answers to six real problems.
keyTakeaway: Interviewers grade the reasoning, not just the formula. Name the variables, count the dominant work, multiply what is nested and add what is sequential, simplify, then give space separately (stack included) and mention the worst case when it differs. Three or four sentences, in that order, every time.
explanation:
In a FAANG style interview, "what's the complexity?" usually comes right after you finish coding, and "O(n)" on its own is a weak answer even when it is right. The interviewer wants to hear that you know WHY: what n is, which part of the code dominates, and what each piece costs. A clear explanation also protects you when you are slightly wrong, because the interviewer can see exactly which step to nudge.

The template has seven steps. First name every variable: n, and m, k, L, V and E when they exist. Then count the dominant work, the loop trips or the recursion's branches and depth. Price each trip and multiply nested costs. Add costs that happen one after another, like a sort before a loop. Drop constants and lower order terms. State space separately, and include the call stack, because that is the cost most often forgotten. Finally, if best, average and worst case differ (hash maps, quicksort, early exits), say which one you gave.

Good answers are short and concrete: "Let n be the number of words and L the longest word. We sort each word, O(L log L), once per word, so O(n · L log L). Space is O(n · L) for the groups." Weak answers skip the variables ("it's linear"), pattern-match on shape ("two loops, so n squared"), or forget space entirely.
